questions.question: Explain why a diet that is low in saturated fat is likely to reduce the risk of CVD.
questions.answer: Less saturated fat lowers blood LDL cholesterol, so less cholesterol is deposited in artery walls and less atheroma forms, reducing CVD risk.

High LDL cholesterol leads to more cholesterol being deposited in artery walls.
This forms atheroma, which narrows arteries and can cause blockages.
A diet low in saturated fat keeps LDL low, so the atheroma and CVD risk are reduced.

questions.question: Explain the effectiveness of the two risk assessment calculators in assessing risk, and whether other factors should be considered.
questions.answer: The calculators give a useful estimate using a few established risk factors, but they are limited by the information entered and omit other factors (such as family history, diet and stress), so other factors should be considered.
steps: Both calculators use established risk factors such as age, blood pressure, cholesterol and smoking, so they give a useful estimate.

Including more factors would make the estimate more accurate, and a doctor should consider them in a full assessment.

questions.question: Explain why the information entered by a person may lead to an underestimate of their 10-year risk of developing CVD.
questions.answer: People may under-report smoking, alcohol, diet or inactivity, or not know their blood pressure or cholesterol, so the calculator gives too low a risk.
steps: People may not know their exact blood pressure or cholesterol level.

questions.question: Suggest why these two risk calculators may not be suitable for everybody to use.
questions.answer: They are based on data from certain populations (age, sex, ethnicity), so they may not be accurate for people outside those groups or with existing conditions.

They may not be accurate for different ages, sexes or ethnic groups.
People who already have CVD or diabetes may need different assessment.

questions.question: Suggest why these risk calculators estimate the 10-year risk of developing CVD.
questions.answer: CVD develops over many years, so a 10-year timescale is a practical period to guide prevention and treatment decisions.
steps: CVD usually develops slowly over many years.
A 10-year period is long enough to show meaningful risk but short enough to be useful.
Doctors can use this to decide whether preventive treatment, such as statins or antihypertensives, is needed.
The timescale matches how risk builds up over years.

questions.question: Explain why eating ginger rhizomes, which have high levels of antioxidants, may help to prevent CVD.
questions.answer: Antioxidants in ginger neutralise free radicals, so LDL cholesterol is less likely to be oxidised, reducing atheroma formation and damage to the endothelium.
steps: Antioxidants donate electrons to neutralise free radicals.
This prevents oxidation of LDL cholesterol.
Oxidised LDL is less likely to build up as atheroma in artery walls.
Less atheroma and less endothelial damage reduce the risk of CVD.

questions.question: Suggest why ginger can be eaten to prevent CVD even though its effectiveness has not been thoroughly tested.
questions.answer: Ginger is a common food with known antioxidant properties and is generally safe to eat in normal amounts, so there is little risk in including it in the diet.
steps: Ginger is a food that has been eaten for a long time with no known harm at normal amounts.
It contains antioxidants that are known to be beneficial for the heart.
So eating it is low risk even before its effect is fully proven.
Eating ginger is low risk, so it can be included before its effectiveness is fully known.

questions.question: Explain how a study should be designed to collect valid and repeatable data to show the effectiveness of ginger in preventing CVD.
questions.answer: Use a large randomised, double-blind controlled trial with a ginger group and a placebo control group, controlled variables, and repeated measurements of CVD markers over time.
steps: Recruit a large, representative sample of people at similar risk of CVD.

Measure CVD markers (blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, endothelial function) at the start and repeatedly, using standard methods so the results are repeatable.
Use statistical analysis to compare the two groups.

questions.question: Explain how atherosclerosis can result in damage to the heart muscle.
questions.answer: Atheroma narrows the coronary arteries, reducing oxygen supply to heart muscle; plaques can rupture and cause clots that block the artery, killing muscle cells in a heart attack.
steps: Atheroma builds up in the walls of the coronary arteries and narrows the lumen.
Less blood flows through, so less oxygen and glucose reach the heart muscle, causing angina during exertion.
Plaques can rupture, releasing material that triggers a blood clot (thrombus).
A clot can completely block the coronary artery, so heart muscle cells die (heart attack), leaving scar tissue and reducing pumping ability.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the structure of an unsaturated fatty acid with the structure of a saturated fatty acid.
questions.answer: Both have a carboxyl group and a hydrocarbon chain; a saturated fatty acid has only single C-C bonds (straight chain), while an unsaturated one has at least one C=C double bond that causes a kink.
steps: Similarity: both are fatty acids with a hydrocarbon chain and a carboxyl (COOH) group at one end.
Contrast: a saturated fatty acid has only single C-C bonds, so its chain is straight.
Contrast: an unsaturated fatty acid has one or more C=C double bonds, which put kinks in the chain.

questions.question: Suggest why a pulmonary embolism, where a clot blocks the pulmonary artery, can cause difficulty in breathing and a rapid heart rate.
questions.answer: The clot blocks blood flow to the lungs, so less gas exchange happens; low oxygen causes faster breathing and the heart beats faster to keep oxygen delivery up.
steps: A clot in the pulmonary artery blocks blood flow to part of the lungs.
Less blood reaches the alveoli, so less oxygen enters the blood and less carbon dioxide is removed.

questions.question: Discuss whether the finding that hibernating bears produce less HSP47, a protein involved in binding platelets to damaged blood vessels, could be useful to humans.
